```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "Feasibility within 90 days: B's core build (poll a directory, check against an expected schedule, validate basic shape, alert to Slack/email/webhook) is low-complexity and suits a one-person, AI-agent build. A's stated differentiator, filing correctly in the country of residence as well, is something no competitor tackles. Even its most advanced competitor calls it 'the hard part.' It would also need accurate tax logic for each country, layered on US PFIC/FBAR/FATCA rules.",
    "Regulatory path to first revenue: A needs IRS e-file Provider (EFIN) authorization with a suitability check, annual IRS software acceptance testing, and GDPR counsel review before launch. Its own open questions list the EFIN timeline as unknown and ask whether self-serve software can legally make country-specific tax calls without a licensed local advisor. B's obligations (a BAA only if handling healthcare EDI, plus standard DPAs) are optional or light for a first non-healthcare customer, and SOC 2 can wait.",
    "Fallback position: if A drops the local-country half, it becomes a US-only product against six sourced self-serve competitors priced from $67 to $799. B is also crowded, but its sourced paid incumbents (Files.com at $199-499/mo, Nodinite at $3,600/yr) show B2B budget for the capability. That leaves room for a cheaper standalone tool for teams that don't run a full managed-file-transfer (MFT) platform.",
    "Sales motion: B is recurring B2B SaaS that can be sold at any time of year to a single team. A has a sourced high-cost channel (Meta lead-gen CPL above the $27.66 blended average in a high-CPC finance vertical) and a once-per-season payment. Neither brief says whether the 90-day window falls inside filing season."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea A's 'Case for' rests on the claim that Atamatax, a solo founder, has 'proven' a one-person PFIC/FBAR tool can 'charge $199-$799 and attract customers.' The only source is Atamatax's own pricing page, which shows list prices, not customers or revenue. The traction claim is therefore effectively unsourced, yet it carries the brief's main argument that a one-person build of this idea is feasible.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate to low confidence. B's demand evidence is notably weak: forum quotes from 2012 and 2016, and a seed HN link with no quoted text. Its own case against (Files.com bundling the same feature, and teams self-building 'with a cron job and a Slack webhook in an afternoon') is well sourced. A has fresher, more vivid demand evidence and clearer willingness-to-pay anchors. B wins mainly because A's scope, liability, and regulatory setup make a paying customer within 90 days unlikely as specified. If A were narrowed to a single country pairing with a clear e-file path, the comparison could flip."
}
```
